newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN chief wants troops in E Slavonia till mid-1997.
newsitem.headline: UN chief wants troops in E Slavonia till mid-1997.

text.p: Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali on Tuesday said U.N. troops should stay in a Serb-held enclave of Croatia until July 15, several months longer than Zagreb originally wanted.
In a report to the Security Council, he said members should also consider keeping U.N. observers in the Eastern Slavonia region bordering Serbia until the end of 1997.

Croatia's President Franjo Tudjman, under pressure from hardliners to get the troops out as soon as possible, has not yet agreed to an extension of U.N. personnel after mid-1997. But the recommendation has been informally approved by Security Council members in the so-called contact group, which sets policy on the former Yugoslavia, diplomats said.
The mandate for the more than 5,000-strong U.N. Transitional Administration in Eastern Slavonia, or UNTAES, expires mid-January.

Tudjman is running for re-election in 1997 and Eastern Slavonia may be an issue. Minority Krajina Serbs seized almost a third of Croatia in a 1991 revolt against independence backed by the Yugoslav army.

The Croatian army reconquered two of three Serb enclaves in blitz offensives in 1995. U.S. envoys then brokered a peaceful solution for Eastern Slavonia to avert another Croatian offensive that would have jeopardised the peace process in neighbouring Bosnia.
There is no date set for the region's transfer back to Croatia, expected to be discussed after the mandate is approved, which requires Zagreb's consent.

In his report Boutros-Ghali said the council should extend the mission soon so it could operate properly without pressure from extremists on all sides. He added that the Croatian government had not met all its commitments and obligations.
"An atmosphere of confrontation and obstruction has developed which appears to be related more to domestic political concerns that to the work of UNTAES," he said.
"This has increased the anxiety and fears of current residents of the region, playing into the hands of Serb hardliners whose obstructionism in turn fuels extremists on the Croatian side."

UNTAES is to prepare the region for reconciliation with Croatia, including economic rehabilitation, law and order, the return of refugees, construction of housing and the organisation of local elections before its mandate expires.

The mission intends to phase in Croatian administrative structures as well as transfer assets from a Serb petroleum company to a Croatian company, which is being delayed by local Serb management, the report said.
An unknown factor, however, is how many Serbs will flee to the rump Yugoslavia -- comprising Serbia and Montenegro -- across the border after Croatia takes over.
